---
title: "Architecture"
---


This section is for anyone who wants to change the package, port it, or check
whether its numbers can be trusted. It assumes you have read the user guide.

## The shape of it

```
src/qdapy/
  contract.py    the exchange contract and the bundled reference files
  read.py        reading and validating exports
  frames.py      the tables every figure is built from
  agreement.py   the six reliability coefficients
  reliability.py intervals, per-code agreement, the kappa diagnostics
  unitizing.py   did the coders mark the same stretches at all
  gamma.py       agreement measured against the best alignment
  progress.py    saturation as a number, and coder drift
  discovery.py   how far from saturation, and how much further to go
  planning.py    how much material a study will need
  reporting.py   the COREQ and SRQR checklists
  stats.py       the inferential statistics
  gg.py          plotnine backend
  sns.py         seaborn backend
  vega.py        the plugin's own Vega-Lite charts, via Altair
  data/          contract + nine samples + expected.json
```

Dependencies run one way only: `gg`, `sns` and `vega` import from `frames`,
`stats` and `agreement`, and never the other way round. `frames` imports
nothing from the package except what pandas gives it. That is what keeps the
three backends from drifting apart, none of them can prepare its own data
without the change showing up in `frames`, where the tests are.

## Why the tables are a separate module

The obvious design puts the data preparation inside each plotting function.
It would work, and it would guarantee that the seaborn bar chart and the
plotnine bar chart eventually disagree about `top=25` or about how ties are
ordered. Splitting the tables out makes that class of bug impossible to write:
there is exactly one `code_counts()`, and both backends call it.

It also means users can have the numbers without the figure, which is what
supplements and reviewers ask for.

## Why the backends load lazily

`import qdapy` does not import matplotlib, seaborn or plotnine. Together they
take about three and a half seconds, and reading a file to compute a
coefficient should not pay for a figure nobody asked for. `__getattr__` in
`__init__.py` imports a backend on first attribute access and caches it in
`globals()`, so `qdapy.gg` behaves like an ordinary attribute from then on.

The cost is that a typo in a backend module surfaces on first use rather than
at import. The test suite touches all three, so CI catches it.

## Reading is a checkpoint, not a convenience

`read()` could have been three lines of `pandas.read_csv`. Instead it checks
the format stamp, the version and the promised columns, and raises
`ContractError` rather than returning something plausible. The reasoning:
a wrong number that stops the script costs an hour, and a wrong number that
does not costs a publication correction.

The version check is deliberately asymmetric. Older versions are read; newer
ones refuse. A newer export may have renamed a column or changed a meaning,
and this package has no way to know which.

## Result objects rather than tuples

`chisq()`, `mds()`, `cluster()` and `ca()` return dataclasses. This is partly
readability, but mostly so that a caveat can travel with the result:
`expected_ok` sits next to the p-value, `goodness` next to the coordinates,
`cophenetic` next to the tree, `inertia_share` next to the map. A tuple
invites unpacking only the first element.

## Why gamma is its own module

`gamma.py` is the only place in the package with an exact combinatorial
search. Finding the best alignment is a set-partitioning problem, NP-hard for
three or more coders, and the implementation is a branch and bound with a
pruning rule and an admissible bound rather than a call to a solver. Keeping
it apart from `unitizing.py` means the cheap measures stay cheap to read, and
the one function with a search budget is obvious.

That budget is deliberate. When the search would exceed it the result is
`nan` with a reason, never the best incumbent found so far. A gamma produced
by a heuristic is not gamma, and a number that is sometimes exact and
sometimes approximate is worse than no number.

## What is deliberately absent

* **No writing.** Nothing here modifies a Zotero library or an export. Coding
  happens in the plugin.
* **No caching of parsed files.** Exports are small and re-reading is cheap;
  a cache would only create a way for the data to go stale mid-session.
* **No plotting defaults beyond a theme.** Colours and labels are arguments,
  because a figure in a paper has to match the rest of the paper.
* **No copyleft dependencies.** Everything qdaPy pulls in is BSD, MIT or PSF,
  so nobody inherits an obligation beyond the AGPL itself, see
  [design decisions](design.qmd).
